name: Z-score
description: Standardizes a value by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, giving the z-score. It tells how many standard deviations the value lies above or below the mean.
notes: Standard deviation must be positive. A positive z is above the mean, negative below. Only comparable across distributions once standardized; it does not by itself give a probability.

name: Raw score from z-score
description: Reverses standardization by multiplying a z-score by the standard deviation and adding the mean, recovering the original raw value that corresponds to that z-score.
notes: This is the inverse of the z-score formula. A positive z returns a value above the mean; keep the same units and standard deviation used to compute the z-score.

name: Standard error of the mean
description: Divides the population standard deviation by the square root of the sample size to give the standard error of the mean, the typical spread of sample means around the true mean.
notes: Sample size n must be positive and larger n shrinks the error only as sqrt(n), so quadrupling n halves it. Uses the population sigma; with a sample std dev the same form applies as an estimate.

name: Confidence interval upper bound
description: Adds the margin of error (z times sigma over root n) to the sample mean to give the upper limit of a confidence interval for the population mean.
notes: This gives only the upper bound; the lower bound subtracts the same margin. The z value fixes the confidence level (1.96 for 95%) and assumes an approximately normal sampling distribution.

name: Standard error of a proportion
description: Computes the standard error of a sample proportion as the square root of p times (1−p) divided by the sample size. It gauges the sampling variability of an estimated proportion.
notes: Proportion p is between 0 and 1 and n must be positive. The standard error is largest at p = 0.5; the normal approximation needs a reasonably large n and not-too-extreme p.

name: Margin of error for a proportion
description: Multiplies a critical z-value by the standard error of a proportion to give the margin of error, the half-width of a confidence interval for a population proportion.
notes: The z value sets the confidence level (1.96 for 95%); p is between 0 and 1 and n positive. The margin is widest near p = 0.5 and relies on the normal approximation.

name: One-sample t-statistic
description: Computes the one-sample t-statistic as the difference between the sample mean and the hypothesized population mean, divided by the standard error (sample std dev over root n). It measures how far the sample mean deviates from the hypothesized value in standard-error units.
notes: Uses the sample standard deviation, so it follows a t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. A p-value requires that distribution, and the test assumes roughly normal data.

name: Cohen's d effect size
description: Computes Cohen's d as the difference between two means divided by the pooled standard deviation. It expresses the size of the difference between groups in standard-deviation units, independent of sample size.
notes: Use a pooled (common) standard deviation for s. Rough benchmarks are 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large; the sign shows which mean is larger.

name: Continuity-Corrected z
description: Computes a continuity-corrected z-score, (x - 0.5 - mu)/sigma, used when approximating a discrete distribution with the normal distribution. The 0.5 adjustment accounts for treating a discrete count as a continuous range.
notes: This particular form subtracts 0.5, appropriate for a right-tail (at least x) probability; use plus 0.5 for a left-tail. mu and sigma are the mean and standard deviation of the approximating normal.

name: z for Sample Mean
description: Computes the z-statistic for a sample mean, (xbar - mu)/(sigma/sqrt(n)), measuring how many standard errors the sample mean xbar lies from the population mean mu. The denominator is the standard error of the mean.
notes: Uses the known population standard deviation sigma, not a sample estimate. It relies on the sampling distribution of the mean being approximately normal.

name: t-Statistic (One Sample)
description: Computes the one-sample t-statistic, (xbar - mu)/(s/sqrt(n)), testing whether a sample mean xbar differs from a hypothesized mean mu. It uses the sample standard deviation s in the standard error.
notes: Unlike the z-statistic it uses the sample standard deviation s, so it follows a t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom. Assumes an approximately normal population.

name: Chi-Square Term
description: Computes a single term of the chi-square statistic, (observed - expected)^2/expected, comparing an observed count with its expected count. Summing this term over all categories gives the chi-square test statistic.
notes: The expected count must be positive and is conventionally at least 5 for the test to be valid. This gives one term only; add the terms across all categories for the full statistic.

name: Cohen's d
description: Computes Cohen's d, an effect size given by (m1 - m2)/sp, the difference between two group means divided by the pooled standard deviation sp. It expresses the gap between groups in standard-deviation units.
notes: sp is the pooled standard deviation and must be positive. Roughly, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 are often read as small, medium and large effects; the sign shows which group is larger.

name: Standard Error of Proportion
description: Computes the standard error of a sample proportion, sqrt(p*(1-p)/n), where p is the observed proportion and n the sample size. It quantifies how much the sample proportion is expected to vary from sample to sample.
notes: p must be between 0 and 1. The normal approximation behind it works best when both n*p and n*(1-p) are reasonably large (commonly at least 5 or 10).

name: CI Half-Width for Proportion
description: Computes the half-width (margin of error) of a confidence interval for a proportion, z*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n), where z is the critical value, p the sample proportion and n the sample size. Adding and subtracting it from p gives the interval.
notes: z sets the confidence level (about 1.96 for 95 percent). p must be between 0 and 1, and the normal approximation requires a sufficiently large sample.

name: Sample Size for Proportion
description: Estimates the minimum sample size needed to estimate a population proportion at a given confidence level and precision. It multiplies z² by the expected variance p(1-p) and divides by the squared margin of error moe².
notes: Use p and moe as decimal fractions, not percents. Set p=0.5 for the most conservative (largest) sample size when p is unknown. Round the result up to a whole number.

name: SE of Difference of Two Means
description: Computes the standard error of the difference between two independent sample means as the square root of s1²/n1 plus s2²/n2. It quantifies the sampling variability of the mean difference.
notes: Assumes the two samples are independent; this unpooled form does not require equal variances. Enter s1 and s2 as standard deviations, not variances.

name: Pooled Proportion
description: Computes the pooled sample proportion by combining the successes from two groups (x1+x2) and dividing by the combined sample sizes (n1+n2). It is used as the common proportion in two-proportion tests.
notes: Used under the null hypothesis that both groups share the same proportion. x1 and x2 are counts of successes, not proportions; the result lies between 0 and 1.

name: Two-Proportion z-Statistic
description: Computes the z-statistic for comparing two sample proportions by dividing their difference by the pooled standard error, which uses the pooled proportion and both sample sizes. It tests whether the two proportions differ.
notes: Enter proportions and the pooled proportion as decimals. The test relies on a large-sample normal approximation and independent groups; compare the result to normal critical values.

name: F-Statistic (Variance Ratio)
description: Computes the F-statistic as the ratio of two sample variances, s1² divided by s2². It is used to test whether two populations have equal variances.
notes: Inputs are standard deviations and are squared internally to variances. Conventionally place the larger variance on top so F is at least 1; compare to F-distribution critical values.

name: Sample Size for Estimating a Mean
description: Computes the minimum sample size needed to estimate a population mean within a target margin of error, using n = (z·σ/E)². A larger standard deviation or tighter margin of error requires a larger sample.
notes: Z is the critical value for the desired confidence level (1.96 for 95% confidence); the result is rounded up since a sample size must be a whole number.

name: Fisher z-Transformation
description: Transforms a Pearson correlation coefficient r into the Fisher z value 0.5*ln((1+r)/(1-r)), which is approximately normally distributed. This stabilizes the variance so correlations can be tested and averaged.
notes: r must be strictly between -1 and 1; values at the boundaries make the logarithm diverge. The transform equals the inverse hyperbolic tangent, artanh(r).

name: One-Sample Proportion Z-Statistic
description: Gives the z-statistic for testing a sample proportion phat against a hypothesized proportion p0, computed as (phat-p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n) with sample size n. It measures how many standard errors the estimate lies from the null value.
notes: Proportions must be between 0 and 1 and n large enough for the normal approximation (roughly n*p0 and n*(1-p0) both at least 5). The standard error uses the null proportion p0, not phat.

name: Standard Error of Skewness
description: Gives the standard error of the sample skewness for a sample of size n, computed as sqrt(6*n*(n-1)/((n-2)*(n+1)*(n+3))). It is used to judge whether an observed skewness differs significantly from zero.
notes: Requires n greater than 2. Compare the sample skewness to roughly plus or minus twice this value; the formula assumes independent observations from a normal population.

name: Margin of Error (Normal)
description: Gives the margin of error for a mean under a normal model, computed as z*sigma/sqrt(n) from the critical value z, standard deviation sigma, and sample size n. It is the half-width of the confidence interval around the sample mean.
notes: z is the standard normal critical value for the confidence level (e.g. 1.96 for 95 percent). This assumes a known sigma; with an estimated standard deviation use a t critical value instead.

name: Sample Size for a Proportion
description: Gives the sample size needed to estimate a proportion within a target margin of error, computed as z^2*p*(1-p)/moe^2 from the critical value z, estimated proportion p, and margin moe. Larger precision demands a larger sample.
notes: p and moe must be between 0 and 1. Use p = 0.5 for the most conservative (largest) sample size when p is unknown; round the result up to the next whole number.

name: Standard Error of Difference (Two Means)
description: Gives the standard error of the difference between two independent sample means, computed as sqrt(s1^2/n1+s2^2/n2) from the group standard deviations s1, s2 and sample sizes n1, n2. It scales the difference in a two-sample z or t test.
notes: The two samples are assumed independent; this unpooled form does not require equal variances (the Welch approach). s1 and s2 are standard deviations, not variances.

name: Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)
description: Scores a model by fit and complexity; lower is better (Akaike 1974).
notes: Only differences between models fitted to the same data matter.

name: Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)
description: Like AIC but penalises parameters by ln n, favouring simpler models on large data (Schwarz 1978).
notes: A BIC difference above 10 is very strong evidence.

name: Durbin–Watson Statistic
description: Tests residuals for first-order autocorrelation: about 2 means none, towards 0 positive, towards 4 negative (Durbin and Watson 1950).
notes: Approximately 2(1 − r₁).

name: Bayes Factor from BIC Difference
description: Approximates the Bayes factor for model 1 over model 0 from their BIC values (Kass and Raftery 1995).
notes: Above 20 is strong evidence, above 150 very strong.

name: Akaike Weight of a Model
description: Turns AIC differences into the probability that each model is the best of the set (Burnham and Anderson 2002).
notes: Use for model averaging instead of picking one winner.

name: Welch's t-Statistic
description: Compares two means without assuming equal variances (Welch 1947); the default two-sample t-test in modern software.
notes: Use the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom with it.

name: Welch–Satterthwaite Degrees of Freedom
description: Gives the approximate degrees of freedom for Welch's t-test.
notes: Usually not a whole number.

name: Welch's t-Test p-Value (Two-Sided)
description: Gives the two-sided p-value for the difference between two means from summary statistics.
notes: Below 0.05 is conventionally called significant — but report the effect size too.

name: Pooled Two-Sample t-Statistic
description: Gives Student's two-sample t assuming equal variances, with n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom.
notes: Prefer Welch's test unless variances are known to be equal.

name: Paired t-Statistic from Differences
description: Tests whether the mean of paired differences is zero, with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
notes: Pairing removes person-to-person variation.

name: One-Sample t-Test p-Value (Two-Sided)
description: Gives the two-sided p-value for testing a sample mean against a hypothesised value.
notes: Assumes roughly normal data or a large sample.

name: z-Test p-Value (Two-Sided)
description: Converts a z statistic into a two-sided p-value.

name: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit p-Value
description: Tests whether observed counts fit expected ones, computing the chi-square statistic and its p-value.
notes: Expected counts should mostly be 5 or more.

name: Chi-Square Test for a 2×2 Table (Yates)
description: Gives the chi-square statistic with Yates' continuity correction for a 2×2 contingency table (1 degree of freedom).
notes: For small counts use Fisher's exact test.

name: Fisher's Exact Test: Probability of One 2×2 Table
expression: hygepdf(a, a + b + c + d, a + b, a + c)
description: Gives the hypergeometric probability of one particular 2×2 table with fixed margins; summing over all tables at least as extreme gives Fisher's exact p-value.
notes: Exact, so valid for small samples.

name: One-Way ANOVA F (Three Groups)
expression: ((count(g1) * (mean(g1) - mean(list(g1, g2, g3)))^2 + count(g2) * (mean(g2) - mean(list(g1, g2, g3)))^2 + count(g3) * (mean(g3) - mean(list(g1, g2, g3)))^2) / 2) / (((count(g1) - 1) * var(g1) + (count(g2) - 1) * var(g2) + (count(g3) - 1) * var(g3)) / (count(g1) + count(g2) + count(g3) - 3))
description: Gives the F statistic for comparing the means of three groups: between-group over within-group variance.
notes: Compare with F(2, N − 3).

name: Sign Test p-Value (Two-Sided)
description: Tests whether positive and negative differences are equally likely, needing no assumption about their size.
notes: Drop ties (zero differences) first.

name: Mann–Whitney U from Rank Sum
description: Converts the rank sum of one group into the Mann–Whitney U statistic for a non-parametric comparison of two groups.
notes: U/(n₁n₂) estimates the probability that group 1 exceeds group 2.

name: Mann–Whitney U z-Approximation
description: Gives the normal-approximation z for the Mann–Whitney U test (no ties).
notes: Adequate when both groups have about 10 or more.

name: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank z-Approximation
description: Gives the normal-approximation z for the Wilcoxon signed-rank test of paired data.
notes: Uses both the sign and size (rank) of differences.

name: Confidence Interval Half-Width for a Mean (t)
description: Gives the ± margin around a sample mean for a t-based confidence interval.
notes: The interval is mean ± this.

name: Confidence Interval for a Variance (Lower)
description: Gives the lower confidence limit for a population variance from a sample (normal data).
notes: Use chi2inv(α/2) in the denominator for the upper limit.

name: Exact (Clopper–Pearson) Confidence Interval for a Proportion (Lower)
description: Gives the lower limit of the exact binomial confidence interval — guaranteed coverage, somewhat conservative.
notes: Upper limit: betainv(1 − α/2, x + 1, n − x).

name: Exact (Clopper–Pearson) Confidence Interval for a Proportion (Upper)
expression: if(x == n, 1, betainv(1 - al / 2, x + 1, n - x))
description: Gives the upper limit of the exact binomial confidence interval.
notes: With zero successes the upper limit is about 3.69/n at α = 0.05; the "rule of three" (3/n) is the one-sided 95 % version.

name: Exact Confidence Interval for a Poisson Count (Lower)
description: Gives the lower limit of the exact confidence interval for the mean of a Poisson count.
notes: Divide by exposure (person-years, area) for a rate.

name: Exact Confidence Interval for a Poisson Count (Upper)
description: Gives the upper limit of the exact confidence interval for the mean of a Poisson count.
notes: With zero events the upper limit is about 3.69 (95 %).

name: Power of a Two-Sided z-Test
description: Gives the probability that a two-sided z-test detects a true difference δ (ignoring the negligible opposite tail).
notes: Aim for 80 % or more when planning a study.

name: Sample Size per Group to Compare Two Means
description: Gives the number of subjects per group needed to detect a difference δ between two means with a given power.
notes: Halving δ quadruples the sample size.

name: Sample Size per Group to Compare Two Proportions
description: Gives the per-group sample size to detect a difference between two proportions (e.g. a clinical trial or A/B test).
notes: Small differences between rare events need very large samples.

name: Hedges' g (Bias-Corrected Effect Size)
description: Corrects Cohen's d for its upward bias in small samples.
notes: The difference is negligible above about 20 per group.

name: Effect Size r from a t-Statistic
description: Converts a t statistic into a correlation-type effect size r.
notes: r ≈ 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large (Cohen).

name: Cohen's h (Difference between Proportions)
description: Gives an effect size for two proportions on the arcsine scale.
notes: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

name: Odds Ratio Confidence Interval (Lower)
expression: exp(ln(a * d / (b * c)) - norminv(1 - al / 2) * sqrt(1 / a + 1 / b + 1 / c + 1 / d))
description: Gives the lower confidence limit of an odds ratio (Woolf's method).
notes: If the interval excludes 1, the association is significant.

name: Relative Risk Confidence Interval (Lower)
expression: exp(ln(a / (a + b) / (c / (c + d))) - norminv(1 - al / 2) * sqrt(1 / a - 1 / (a + b) + 1 / c - 1 / (c + d)))
description: Gives the lower confidence limit of a risk ratio from a cohort study (log method).
notes: Use + instead of − for the upper limit.

name: Šidák-Corrected Significance Level
description: Gives the per-test significance level that keeps the chance of any false positive at α across m independent tests.
notes: Slightly less strict than Bonferroni (α/m).

name: Benjamini–Hochberg Critical Value
description: Gives the threshold for the i-th smallest p-value; reject all hypotheses up to the largest i whose p-value falls below it (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).
notes: Controls the expected share of false discoveries, not the chance of any.

name: Grubbs' Test Statistic
description: Gives the largest standardised deviation in a sample, for testing whether it is an outlier (Grubbs 1950).
notes: Compare with the Grubbs critical value for n; assumes normal data.

name: Cronbach's Alpha
description: Measures the internal consistency of a questionnaire scale (Cronbach 1951).
notes: Above 0.7 is usually acceptable; above 0.95 may mean redundant items.

name: Bland–Altman Upper Limit of Agreement
description: Gives the upper 95 % limit of agreement between two measurement methods (Bland and Altman 1986).
notes: Subtract instead of add for the lower limit.

name: Kolmogorov–Smirnov Critical Value (Large Sample)
description: Gives the approximate 5 % critical value of the one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic D.
notes: Use tables for n below about 35.

name: Standard Error of the Median
description: Gives the standard error of a sample median for normal data: about 25 % larger than that of the mean.
notes: The median wins for heavy-tailed data.

name: Design Effect for Cluster Sampling
description: Gives how much a clustered sample inflates the variance compared with simple random sampling.
notes: Multiply the simple-random sample size by it.

name: Finite Population Correction
description: Gives the factor that shrinks standard errors when the sample is a sizeable part of a finite population.
notes: Negligible when n is under about 5 % of N.

name: Fisher's Method for Combining p-Values
description: Combines p-values from independent tests of the same hypothesis into one overall p-value (Fisher 1925).
notes: Several weak results can be jointly significant.

name: Stouffer's Combined z
description: Combines z scores from independent studies into one (Stouffer 1949); weighted versions are used in meta-analysis.
notes: Convert to a p-value with the normal distribution.

name: Likelihood-Ratio Test p-Value
description: Tests whether adding parameters significantly improves a model's fit (Wilks' theorem).
notes: Models must be nested.

name: Nelson–Aalen Cumulative Hazard

variables.label: Number at risk at each time

description: Estimates the cumulative hazard from event times (Nelson 1972, Aalen 1978); exp(−H) approximates survival.
notes: Handles censoring like Kaplan–Meier.

name: Log-Rank Test Chi-Square (Two Groups)
description: Gives the log-rank statistic comparing two survival curves; compare with χ² on 1 degree of freedom.
notes: E₁ and V come from summing over event times.

name: Life-Table Probability of Dying from a Death Rate

variables.label: Fraction of the year lived by those dying

description: Converts a central death rate mₓ into the probability qₓ of dying within the year, as when building a life table.
notes: With aₓ = ½, qₓ ≈ mₓ/(1 + ½mₓ).

name: Number of Events Needed (Schoenfeld)
description: Gives how many events (not patients) a survival trial needs to detect a hazard ratio (Schoenfeld 1983).
notes: Divide by the expected event rate for the number of patients.

name: Laplace's Rule of Succession
description: Gives the probability the next trial succeeds after k successes in n, starting from a uniform prior (Laplace 1814).
notes: Never gives exactly 0 or 1.

name: Beta Posterior Credible Interval (Lower)
expression: betainv(al / 2, a0 + k, b0 + n - k)
description: Gives the lower limit of an equal-tailed Bayesian credible interval for a proportion.
notes: Upper limit: betainv(1 − α/2, …).

name: Gamma–Poisson Posterior Mean Rate
description: Updates a gamma prior on a Poisson rate with observed counts and gives the posterior mean.
notes: The prior acts like β intervals with α events.

name: Proportional Stratified Allocation
description: Gives the sample size for a stratum in proportion to its population share.
notes: Round so the strata add up to n.

name: Neyman Optimal Allocation
expression: n * at(nh, k) * at(sh, k) / sum(nh * sh)
description: Gives the sample size for stratum k that minimises variance for a fixed total: more sampling in larger and more variable strata (Neyman 1934).
notes: Needs estimates of each stratum's spread.

name: Sample Size with Finite Population Correction

variables.label: Sample size for an infinite population

description: Reduces a required sample size when the population is small.
notes: 385 (±5 %, 95 %) becomes 323 for a population of 2000.

name: Sample Size to Detect a Correlation
expression: ceil(((norminv(1 - al / 2) + norminv(pw)) / (0.5 * ln((1 + r) / (1 - r))))^2 + 3)
description: Gives the number of pairs needed to detect a correlation r with a two-sided test, via Fisher's z.
notes: r = 0.3 needs about 85 pairs at 80 % power.

name: Spearman–Brown Prophecy Formula
description: Predicts the reliability of a test lengthened (or shortened) k times with similar items.
notes: Doubling a 0.7 test gives about 0.82.

name: Standard Error of Measurement
description: Gives the typical error in an individual's observed score from the test's reliability.
notes: ±2 SEM gives about a 95 % band around a score.

name: Minimal Detectable Change (95 %)
description: Gives the smallest change between two measurements that exceeds measurement error with 95 % confidence.
notes: Used in rehabilitation and clinical outcome scales.

name: Intraclass Correlation ICC(1)
description: Gives the reliability of single ratings from a one-way random-effects ANOVA (Shrout and Fleiss 1979).
notes: Above 0.75 good, above 0.9 excellent (Koo and Li 2016).

name: Kruskal–Wallis H Statistic
description: Gives the non-parametric one-way ANOVA statistic on ranks (Kruskal and Wallis 1952); compare with χ² on k − 1 degrees of freedom.
notes: Rank all observations together first (no ties assumed).

name: Friedman Test Statistic
description: Gives the non-parametric repeated-measures statistic on within-subject ranks (Friedman 1937); compare with χ² on k − 1 degrees of freedom.
notes: Each subject ranks the k treatments from 1 to k.

name: Wald–Wolfowitz Runs Test z
description: Tests whether a sequence of two kinds of outcomes is random by counting runs; too few runs suggests clustering, too many alternation.
notes: Normal approximation for n₁, n₂ above about 10.

name: Phi Coefficient (2×2 Table)
expression: (a * d - b * c) / sqrt((a + b) * (c + d) * (a + c) * (b + d))
description: Gives the correlation between two binary variables from a 2×2 table.
notes: φ² = χ²/N.

name: Yule's Q
expression: (a * d - b * c) / (a * d + b * c)
description: Gives a measure of association for a 2×2 table from −1 to 1, a transformation of the odds ratio: (OR − 1)/(OR + 1).
notes: Reaches ±1 when any cell is zero.

name: Cramér's V
description: Gives the strength of association in a contingency table of any size, from 0 to 1.
notes: About 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large for 2×2.

name: G-Test (Log-Likelihood Ratio) Statistic
description: Gives the likelihood-ratio alternative to Pearson's chi-square for goodness of fit; compare with χ².
notes: Observed counts must be positive.

name: Eta Squared (ANOVA Effect Size)
description: Gives the share of total variance explained by group membership.
notes: 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large.

name: Omega Squared (ANOVA Effect Size)
description: Gives a less biased estimate of explained variance than eta squared.
notes: Can be slightly negative for tiny effects (report as 0).

name: Cohen's f from Eta Squared
description: Converts eta squared into Cohen's f, used in ANOVA power analysis.
notes: 0.10 small, 0.25 medium, 0.40 large.

name: Glass's Delta
description: Gives a standardised mean difference using only the control group's standard deviation, useful when treatment changes the spread.
notes: Compare Cohen's d, which pools both SDs.

name: Paired Effect Size (Cohen's dz)
description: Gives the effect size for paired data: mean difference over the standard deviation of differences.
notes: Used for power analysis of paired designs.

name: Confidence Interval for a Difference in Proportions (Lower)
description: Gives the lower Wald confidence limit for the difference between two independent proportions.
notes: Use + for the upper limit; Newcombe's method is better for small samples.

name: Comparing Two Poisson Rates (z-Test)
description: Tests whether two event rates differ, using a normal approximation for Poisson counts.
notes: For small counts use an exact binomial test on x₁ given x₁ + x₂.

name: Confidence Interval for a Median: Rank of the Lower Limit
description: Gives which ordered observation is the lower limit of a distribution-free confidence interval for the median.
notes: The upper limit is the observation with rank n + 1 − lower.

name: Normal Tolerance Interval Factor (Two-Sided, Howe)
expression: sqrt((n - 1) * (1 + 1 / n) * norminv((1 + pc) / 2)^2 / chi2inv(1 - cf, n - 1))
description: Gives k so that mean ± k·s covers a chosen proportion of a normal population with a chosen confidence (Howe 1969).
notes: Wider than a confidence interval for the mean.

name: Minimum Detectable Effect for an A/B Test
expression: (norminv(1 - al / 2) + norminv(pw)) * sqrt(2 * p * (1 - p) / n)
description: Gives the smallest absolute change in conversion rate an A/B test of a given size can reliably detect.
notes: Divide by p for the relative lift.

name: Bayesian A/B: Probability B Beats A (Normal Approximation)
description: Approximates the posterior probability that variant B has the higher conversion rate, using uniform Beta priors.
notes: Exact values need numerical integration; this is close for large samples.

name: Bayesian Average Rating
description: Shrinks an item's average rating towards a prior mean, so items with few ratings are not over-ranked.
notes: Used by review sites and film databases.

name: Poll Margin of Error with Design Effect
expression: norminv(1 - al / 2) * sqrt(deff * p * (1 - p) / n) * 100
description: Gives the margin of error of a survey proportion, inflated for weighting or clustering.
notes: A simple random sample of 1000 gives ±3.1 points; weighting often adds 20–50 %.

name: Item Response (3-Parameter Logistic)
description: Gives the probability of a correct answer for a person of ability θ in item response theory (Birnbaum 1968).
notes: With c = 0 it is the two-parameter model.

name: Item Discrimination Index
description: Compares how often high and low scorers answer an item correctly; above 0.3 is good, below 0.2 needs revision.
notes: Groups are often the top and bottom 27 %.

name: Kuder–Richardson 20 Reliability
description: Gives the internal-consistency reliability of a test with right/wrong items (Kuder and Richardson 1937).
notes: Cronbach's alpha generalises it to any item scores.

name: T-Score from z-Score
description: Converts a z-score to a T-score (mean 50, SD 10), common in psychological and bone-density reports.
notes: IQ-style scales use 100 + 15z.

name: Stanine from z-Score
description: Converts a z-score to a stanine (standard nine) from 1 to 9, used in educational testing.
notes: Each stanine is half a standard deviation wide.

name: Mean Estimated from Median and Quartiles (Wan)
description: Estimates a sample mean from the median and quartiles for meta-analysis (Wan et al. 2014).
notes: Pair with SD ≈ (Q3 − Q1)/1.35 for large samples.

name: Heterogeneity I² (Meta-Analysis)
description: Gives the share of variation across studies due to real differences rather than chance (Higgins and Thompson 2002).
notes: 25 % low, 50 % moderate, 75 % high.

name: Cochran's Q from Study Estimates
expression: sum((y - sum(y / se^2) / sum(1 / se^2))^2 / se^2)
description: Gives the weighted sum of squared deviations of study results from the pooled estimate, the basis of heterogeneity tests.
notes: Compare with χ² on k − 1 degrees of freedom.

name: Between-Study Variance τ² (DerSimonian–Laird)
expression: max(0, (q - (count(se) - 1)) / (sum(1 / se^2) - sum(1 / se^4) / sum(1 / se^2)))
description: Estimates the variance of true effects across studies for a random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian and Laird 1986).
notes: Add τ² to each study's variance for random-effects weights.

name: Relative Lift of a Variant
description: Gives the percentage improvement of a variant over the control in an experiment.
notes: Always report with a confidence interval.
